title: Token Anatomy Workbench — usability notes & low-fi wireframes
content:
Context:
Quick round of hallway usability + a remote guerrilla test (5 participants: 3 ML engineers, 1 product manager, 1 SRE) for the "Token Anatomy Workbench" concept — a focused view for token-level cost & latency forensics intended to be used during incident triage and iterative perf tuning. Goal: validate the high-level information hierarchy and interactions before investing in hi-fi mocks or data plumbing.

High-level goal and hypothesis:
- Goal: give engineers an investigative surface to answer “why did this invocation cost X / take Y ms?” within 1–2 clicks and support rapid hypothesis-to-action (re-run, pinning cache, fallback policy).
- Hypothesis: surfacing token ancestry (prompt vs completion vs system), per-token kernel/call-path attribution, and quick filters (model variant, quantization, batch size) will reduce mean time to root-cause for cost/latency regressions.

Test tasks given to participants (short):
1) Find the token that first caused a p95 spike in a selected invocation and identify its origin (user prompt / system / tool).
2) Compare two invocations and find difference in token mix causing a 2x cost increase.
3) Create a lightweight rule to pin a cheaper quantized variant for future invocations that match a pattern.

Top-level findings (observational):
- Overall mental model: participants expected a timeline-first view (time waterfall) but wanted token breakdown to map directly to timeline slices — i.e., they expect clicking a time region to highlight tokens, not the other way around.
- Affordance confusion: the initial left-rail timeline widget and center waterfall were both clickable; users tried clicking the waterfall expecting a time scrub. We need a clear affordance (scrubber handle / hover preview).
- Attribution clarity: developers wanted explicit labels for attribution (kernel:attention, kernel:kv-cache-miss, runtime:wait-for-lock, routing:fallthrough) — abbreviations were confusing.
- Copy matters: short phrases like “token cost” vs “token charge” produced different expectations; prefer “token charge (USD)” in monetary contexts and “token compute (ms/step)” for perf.
- Quick actions are essential: pin-to-variant, replay-in-dev, open-in-trace. If quick action not present in the token row, participants tried right-click or expected keyboard shortcuts.

Concrete usability issues to address in next iteration:
- Interaction: make timeline scrub primary — tapping a waterfall block should scrub timeline and show trace overlay.
- Visibility: token names that are long (tool outputs) should truncate but offer inline expansion via hover + keyboard (VT100-friendly).
- Onboarding: first-run tooltip explaining the three primary panes (timeline, token waterfall, controls).
- Accessibility: ensure keyboard-only flow for selecting tokens and triggering actions; ensure color contrast on heatmap palettes.

Low-fi wireframe descriptions (notes for designers/devs):
- Main layout: 3-column responsive grid
  * Left: invocation list + compact timeline (p50/p95 bands) with region selection.
  * Middle (primary): token waterfall — each row = token group (origin:prompt/system/tool), columns = micro-stages (prep -> kernel exec -> kv access -> serialize). Width ~ token duration; color = latency contributor; small currency icon shows cost on hover. Rows can be nested (fold/unfold) to show subtokenization.
  * Right: contextual controls + quick actions (pin variant, rerun with modified prompt, open trace, annotate). Also shows top-3 hypothesis suggestions from Optimize engine (batch/quantize/cache).

- Drill mode: double-click a token row to open modal with: token byte-level view, embedding distance to nearest cache hit, kernel selection graph, call stack of runtime events, and suggested mitigations (auto-generated). Modal also has “Create ticket” quick-populate with fields for stack, example invocation, suggested fix.

- Collaboration: inline annotations attached to tokens (comment threads) and session links. Each annotation shows author and timestamp; allow pinning to console route. Participants liked the idea of saving a “triage snapshot” (timestamped link + filtered view).

Telemetry & instrumentation (must-have events):
- invocation.viewed (invocation_id, model_variant, region, user_id)
- token.row.clicked (token_id, origin, latency_ms, cost_cents)
- timeline.region.selected (start_ms, end_ms, p50, p95)
- action.pin_variant (invocation_id, variant_id)
- modal.opened (token_id, duration_open_ms)
- snapshot.saved (user_id, snapshot_id, filter_hash)
Notes: include token origin enums and canonical cost units in event schema.

Acceptance criteria for MVP (short):
1) Select an invocation, scrub a timeline region, and see token waterfall filtered to that region.
2) Click a token to open drill modal with kernel-level attribution and quick actions.
3) Save a triage snapshot and produce a stable link that restores filters and modal state.
4) Telemetry for token.row.clicked and snapshot.saved emitted.

Backlog & priorities (rough):
- P0 (sprint): timeline scrub + waterfall sync, token drill modal (kernel attribution), pin-to-variant action, telemetry. (3 devs, 3 wks)
- P1: collaborative annotations, triage snapshot share link, replay-in-dev button (dev infra work). (2 devs, 2 sprints)
- P2: heuristic-based suggestions from Optimize, mobile layout adjustments, a11y audit. (1–2 sprints)

Design alternatives discussed (pros / cons):
- Option A: token-first primary (current prototype) — pros: immediate token details; cons: users wanted timeline-first so risk of friction.
- Option B: timeline-first primary (recommended) — pros: better fit for triage/time-based debugging; cons: more complex time scrub interactions.
- Option C: blended (compact timeline overlaid on waterfall) — pros: single surface; cons: potential visual clutter and harder a11y.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- How to display cost for mixed-currency customer accounts? (show token compute + account currency)
- Which kernel-level labels are stable across runtime builds? We need to define canonical attribution taxonomy with runtime team.
- Snapshot retention policy — default 30 days? legal input needed.
- Do we allow external collaborators (customers) to comment on snapshots in hosted product? (privacy)

Next steps (owners):
- Maya: prepare hi-fi wireframe for timeline-first layout and handoff doc to design (due 2026-02-24).
- Ethan: propose minimal telemetry schema and PR to analytics repo (due 2026-02-17).
- Priya: sync with runtime on canonical attribution labels and a short glossary doc (due 2026-02-21).
- Luis: spike on replay-in-dev feasibility (estimate infra changes; due 2026-03-03).

Quick notes to designers / PMs (informal):
- Keep the middle pane laser-focused: engineers used it like a debugger, not a dashboard. Avoid adding summary cards that pull attention away.
- Microcopy: use plain terms for actions: "Pin cheaper variant", "Replay in dev", "Highlight cache miss".
- Performance budget: waterfall rendering should keep < 80ms frame for 200 token rows; consider canvas rendering or virtualization.

Raw snippets from participant sessions (quote-y):
- "I want to scrub the time — I don't want to click each token to see when it happened." — SRE
- "Show me the cheapest token and the slowest token in the same view." — ML Eng
- "A 'create bug with repro' button would save me 15 minutes." — PM

Attachments / sketches included in next pass: low-fi PNGs and Figma links (will attach after design pass).


Notes end.
